summary: Describes an experimental policy for using the 233/8 block of the multicast address space as a statically assigned set, with addresses derived from autonomous system numbers. It is an experimental protocol, and it was replaced by RFC 3180.

eli5.summary: Each network owner gets a ready-made set of group addresses based on their own number, so no one needs to ask.

questions: how are multicast addresses assigned in 233/8
subtitle: Static multicast addresses automatically assigned based on Autonomous System numbers.

tldr.problem: Multicast applications need group addresses, but there was no standard static allocation scheme, and dynamic allocation mechanisms were not universally accepted or practical for applications requiring fixed addresses.
tldr.mechanism: GLOP automatically assigns multicast addresses in the 233/8 block using the formula 233.AS-high.AS-low/24, where AS is the network's registered Autonomous System number. Each AS gets a /24 block of 256 addresses with no registration required.
tldr.outcome: This experimental allocation ran for one year starting in 2000. While it provided a quick way to bootstrap multicast without dynamic protocols, wider multicast adoption followed other paths, and RFC 3180 replaced it.

today: RFC 2770 is Experimental and was succeeded by RFC 3180. The GLOP allocation provides statically assigned multicast addresses alongside dynamic allocation schemes for modern multicast deployments.

sections.title: The Problem
sections.content: Multicast addresses are used to send messages to groups of computers at once. Traditionally, these addresses were allocated dynamically—someone asked a server for an address when they needed one. But many content distributors and applications need group addresses that are stable and known ahead of time, not allocated on demand. The RFC notes that without a coherent multicast address allocation scheme, the Internet lacked a standard way to handle this.
sections.eli5: Multicast lets one computer send to many, but you need a group address. Some things need their group address to never change.

sections.title: How GLOP Works
sections.content:
GLOP ("Global Multicast Group Organization Proposal") uses the 233/8 multicast address block. The formula is simple: the first octet is 233, the next two octets are the Autonomous System (AS) number (split into high and low bytes), and the last octet is available for local use. For example, AS 5662 maps to 233.22.30/24. The network registry already maintains the list of registered AS numbers, so no new registration is needed.

Each Autonomous System gets exactly 256 multicast addresses (a /24 block) to allocate locally. Private AS numbers (RFC 1930) are reserved for future allocation.
sections.eli5: Every network owner has a number (an Autonomous System number). GLOP gives them group addresses based on that number, so they automatically get some multicast group numbers.

sections.title: Experimental Trial and Transition
sections.content: The IANA allocated 233/8 for a one-year experimental period. The experiment ran in parallel with other multicast allocation proposals. After the trial, applications with fixed multicast requirements could use the static 233/8 addresses, while dynamic allocation schemes like MADCAP or single-source multicast could serve other needs.
sections.eli5: This was a one-year experiment to see if giving each network owner some group numbers would work. Other methods could also provide multicast addresses.
